claim: Before designing, rewrite the client's brief into a problem statement with three parts: what the user is trying to do, what currently blocks them, and the business metric that suffers. If you can only write the deliverable, you have not got a brief yet.
why: Briefs arrive named after artefacts ('a new site with a CMS'), which locks you into a solution before anyone has checked whether it addresses the loss the client is actually feeling.
when: Intake, discovery calls, and proposal writing for any client engagement.
fails: Genuine execution-only work — a rebrand rollout or a spec handed down from an in-house team that already ran discovery — where re-litigating the problem wastes the client's time.

claim: When a catalogue is large and sales are falling, treat it as a findability failure first: fix search and re-cut the category taxonomy around how customers describe what they want, and only then style the pages.
why: If shoppers can't reach the product, no amount of visual polish on the product page gets used; the drop-off happens upstream of the pixels.
when: E-commerce or content sites with high item counts and shallow or seller-organised navigation.
fails: Small catalogues where everything is reachable in a click or two — there the bottleneck is trust and presentation, not discovery.

claim: Ship every screen against two pass/fail questions: is all the information a visitor needs visible and legibly laid out, and is the single next action unmistakable? Fix any 'no' before touching aesthetics.
why: These two properties are what actually move conversion, and they are independent of how attractive the page is.
when: Reviewing landing pages, checkout steps, and any conversion-critical flow.
fails: Brand, editorial, or portfolio surfaces where the goal is impression rather than an immediate action — the second question has no clean answer there.

claim: Do not use visual quality as a proxy for effectiveness. Judge a reference page by whether its structure and calls to action work, and be willing to borrow the structure of a page you find ugly.
why: Funnel-builder pages are plainly unattractive yet perform, which proves the two properties are separable — attractiveness is neither necessary nor sufficient.
when: Competitive teardowns, gathering references, and arguing against a redesign that is purely cosmetic.
fails: Premium and luxury positioning, where perceived craft is itself part of the value proposition being sold.

claim: Expect clients to evaluate you on UI and to be paid on UX outcomes. Deliver the visual quality that wins the approval, but drive the decisions from the flow, and present the work as 'here is the problem this solves' rather than 'here is the look'.
why: The two audiences differ — the client judges the mockup in the room, their customers judge the flow later — and only the second one produces the results you get rehired for.
when: Client presentations, design rationale, and case-study writing.

claim: Pick your niche by the recurring problem you solve, not only by the industry you serve — 'I fix product discovery for large catalogues' travels further than 'I build boutique sites'.
why: A problem-shaped niche lets you reuse a diagnosis and a method across sectors, while an industry-shaped one caps you at that sector's budget.
when: Positioning a freelance or studio practice and choosing which case studies to lead with.
fails: Very early on, when you have no repeat pattern yet and an industry niche is the faster way to get referrals.

claim: Write the case study as problem -> diagnosis -> intervention -> result, and name the non-visual intervention explicitly (search, taxonomy, step order) instead of leading with before-and-after screenshots.
why: The chapter's whole demonstration is that the valuable part of the work is the diagnosis; a screenshot-led case study hides exactly the thing that justifies the fee.
when: Building a portfolio intended to win higher-value client work.

claim: Scope a design deliverable as a system, not a screen: for any feature, enumerate its states (empty, loading, hover, error, success, populated) and the flows that connect it to the rest of the product before styling anything.
why: Polish on a single screen is only decoration; the perceived quality of a product comes from whether every state and transition is accounted for, so users never hit a dead end.
when: Designing any interactive feature inside a real product, or building portfolio work meant to demonstrate design ability.
fails: One-off marketing or brand surfaces (a landing page, a campaign site) where there is genuinely little state and visual craft is the deliverable.

claim: Design the empty state as an onboarding surface: when a user creates a new container (project, board, workspace), show guidance on the first action to take rather than a blank region.
why: The empty state is the user's first contact with a feature; leaving it blank shifts the burden of figuring out what to do onto the user, while guidance makes the product feel effortless.
when: Any collection view or container that begins with zero items.

claim: Use hover to reveal secondary context about an item instead of forcing a navigation or click to see it.
why: Surfacing detail in place keeps the user oriented in their current view and reduces the number of steps needed to make a decision.
when: Dense list or board views on pointer devices where each row carries more metadata than fits inline.
fails: Touch-only contexts where hover does not exist, or when the hidden information is essential rather than supplementary — then it must be visible by default.

claim: Make animation carry information: reserve motion for moments where something changed state, and keep it subtle enough that it reports the change without demanding attention.
why: Motion tied to a state change confirms the system registered an action; decorative motion adds noise and slows perceived responsiveness.
when: Status changes, item transitions, and any feedback after a user action.
fails: Applying the same motion treatment decoratively across static elements, which drains it of signalling value.

claim: Build portfolio cases around a problem and the system that resolves it — lead with the flows, states, and decisions, and treat the final visuals as evidence rather than the case itself.
why: Hiring evaluates whether a designer can reason about product behaviour; a gallery of polished screens does not demonstrate that reasoning.
when: Assembling a portfolio or case study intended to get design work.
fails: Roles explicitly scoped to visual or brand design, where craft samples are the point.

claim: When a product feels good, diagnose the actual cause before copying it: separate the aesthetic layer from the structural decisions (information hierarchy, state coverage, flow length) and reproduce the structure.
why: Teams routinely copy the visual style of an admired product and get none of the feel, because the feel came from system decisions the style merely dressed.
when: Doing competitive teardowns or drawing inspiration from a benchmark product.

claim: Design in screens and sequences, not in stacked sections: before drawing a screen, write down the state the user arrived from and the state they should be able to reach next.
why: Sections are a page-composition unit that assumes a passive reader scrolling; app users are mid-task, so each screen only makes sense relative to the step before and after it.
when: Designing product/app surfaces where users are completing tasks — dashboards, tools, settings, anything with actions.
fails: Marketing pages and content-first sites, where the section-stack model is the correct one and no task state carries between blocks.

claim: After a create action, do not dismiss the modal back to an empty state — chain directly into the step that makes the created object useful (invite members, add items, set the first rule).
why: A freshly created empty container has no value on its own; the moment right after creation is when the user's intent and context are highest, so it is the cheapest place to ask for the next input.
when: Any 'create new X' flow where X is a container that needs contents or collaborators before it does anything.
fails: When the created object is complete and self-sufficient on creation, where an extra step is friction with no payoff.

claim: Any chained follow-up step must carry an explicit skip or dismiss control, not just a close button.
why: Chaining is a suggestion about likely intent, not a requirement; without a visible skip the helpful next step reads as a mandatory gate and users start fighting the flow.
when: Post-creation prompts, onboarding sequences, and any step the system inserted rather than the user requesting.
fails: Steps that are genuinely required for the object to be valid or safe (payment, permissions, legally required consent) — those should be gates, and should look like gates.

claim: Treat a single feature entry point as a sequence of small decisions: decompose 'contact the applicant' into choose message -> confirm recipients -> send, and design each handoff, rather than cramming it into one screen.
why: Breaking a task into discrete decisions keeps each screen to one question, which is easier to answer and easier to reverse, and it exposes the transitions as things you can actually design.
when: Actions with more than one variable to resolve (content, recipients, timing, scope).
fails: Trivial single-variable actions, where splitting them adds clicks and modal churn for no clarity gain.

claim: Before the final irreversible step, insert a widening question that lets the user extend the action to similar targets — e.g. 'add any other recipients before sending?'
why: Users doing one instance of a repetitive task usually have several; catching that before send collapses N passes through the flow into one and avoids near-duplicate sends.
when: Batchable actions on list items — messaging, tagging, rejecting, exporting from a table or queue.
fails: High-stakes or personalised actions where batching invites mistakes, or where each instance needs distinct content.

claim: Audit an existing flow by walking it as a user and marking every point where the interface stops and hands control back with nothing suggested — each dead end is a missing next step.
why: Flow gaps are invisible in static screen mockups and only surface when the screens are viewed in order as a sequence.
when: Reviewing or critiquing a designed feature before build.

claim: Study shipped flows from mature products by recording them step by step and noting where each step could have terminated but did not — use that as the reference for your own chaining.
why: The chaining decisions in polished products are deliberate and legible once you look at ordering rather than visual style.
when: Building a pattern library or deciding how far to chain a flow of your own.

claim: Any screen offering a fixed set of choices must also offer a way to enter a choice that is not on the list — a search field, a text input, or an 'other' option.
why: A preset list is a designer's guess at the common cases; a user whose real answer is absent has no path forward and the flow dead-ends.
when: Selection screens built from curated presets — allergies, dietary needs, interests, tags, categories, countries — where the true option space is larger than what fits on screen.
fails: The option set is genuinely closed and exhaustive (blood type, star rating, yes/no), where a free-text escape hatch adds noise and produces unusable data.

claim: Give every data-collection step an explicit opt-out — a 'Skip', 'None of these', or 'I don't have any' control — rather than assuming every user has something to enter.
why: The null case is a legitimate answer, and without a control that expresses it the user either gets blocked or is forced to enter something false.
when: Onboarding steps, preference capture, and any optional profile field presented as a required-feeling screen.
fails: The step is genuinely required for the product to function or for legal/safety reasons — then the answer is to explain why, not to add a skip.

claim: Sketch the whole flow as labelled boxes with arrows on paper before designing any individual screen, and walk each user type through it end to end.
why: Gaps are relational — they live between screens and in branches you never drew — so they are invisible while you are polishing one screen at a time, but obvious when the whole path is laid out at once.
when: Starting any multi-screen feature, especially onboarding and setup wizards.
fails: Single-screen changes or tightly-scoped component work where there is no branching path to map.

claim: Walk the flow as at least three personas — the typical user, the user whose answer is outside your presets, and the user with no answer at all — and confirm each has a forward path from every screen.
why: Designers naturally prototype the happy path; the edge personas are exactly the ones who hit dead ends, and naming them turns an abstract 'consider edge cases' into a checkable pass.
when: Reviewing a flow sketch or a built prototype before handoff.

claim: Audit each screen for the four commonly-omitted layers: navigation and exit routes, non-default states (empty, loading, error, no-results), interactive feedback (hover, pressed, focus, disabled), and micro-interactions on state change.
why: These are the parts that don't show up in a static mockup, so they get skipped in design and improvised in code — which is where a build stops feeling production-ready.
when: Pre-handoff review of any screen set, and when judging whether a design file is actually complete.

claim: Place secondary affordances where their host element already is: a filter control inside or adjacent to the search field, a save action in the top app bar next to the screen title.
why: Co-locating a modifier with the thing it modifies means the user finds it while already looking at the relevant element, instead of scanning the page for it.
when: Screens with a primary input or content region that supports refinement or persistence actions.
fails: When the secondary action is destructive or high-stakes — proximity to a frequently-tapped control then causes mis-taps.

claim: Treat small affordances as flow-completing, not decorative: a missing filter or save control is the same class of defect as a missing screen, just cheaper to fix.
why: The user's felt experience is continuous; friction from a missing one-tap shortcut compounds across a session even though it never appears as a broken screen.
when: Prioritising design polish against feature work.
fails: When adding affordances outpaces the underlying functionality — controls that look actionable but do nothing are worse than their absence.

claim: Put persistent, globally-scoped controls — primary navigation, account/profile, search — in the sidebar rather than repeating them per page.
why: A fixed spine gives users one stable place to orient from, so they never hunt for global actions when the main pane changes.
when: Dashboard or app-shell layouts where content swaps but the surrounding chrome stays put.
fails: Profile and search are equally valid in a top bar; on narrow or content-first layouts a top bar may be the better home.

claim: Reserve the top slot of the sidebar for the account/workspace switcher rather than a static logo, and render it as avatar + name + a chevron.
why: The top slot is the most valuable real estate, so give it to something interactive; an avatar is recognized faster than text, and the chevron signals the row opens something.
when: Logged-in product UIs where users switch accounts, workspaces, or reach settings often.
fails: Marketing-adjacent or multi-tenant surfaces where brand identity must anchor the top, or single-account tools with nothing to switch between.

claim: Build every nav link as a recognizable icon plus a short one-or-two-word label, never label-only.
why: The icon carries the meaning when the label is hidden, which is what makes the rail collapsible; it also gives badges and chips a fixed anchor point.
when: Any vertical nav list, especially one intended to collapse to an icon rail or carry counts and status chips.
fails: Concepts with no conventional icon — a vague or invented glyph is worse than text alone once collapsed.

claim: Decide on collapsibility before styling links, because it constrains the link anatomy.
why: A collapsed rail keeps only the icon, so a design that leans on text length or a wide hit area has to be rebuilt rather than tightened.
when: Sidebars in data-dense products where users will want to reclaim horizontal space.

claim: Cluster nav links into small labelled groups by task relatedness instead of listing them flat.
why: Grouping lets a user scan a handful of categories rather than every item, which is the concrete way you reduce cognitive load in navigation.
when: Once the link count passes roughly five to seven items.

claim: Push low-frequency destinations like Settings and Help to a bottom-pinned group, separated from the main nav.
why: Vertical position should track usage frequency — rarely-touched items shouldn't compete with daily ones for the top of the scan path.
when: Sidebars containing both workflow destinations and account/support utilities.

claim: When a section grows past what fits comfortably, nest its children in an expandable dropdown rather than lengthening the flat list.
why: Nesting keeps the visible list short and preserves the top-level structure as the list scales.
when: Products with deep hierarchies or many sub-destinations under one concept.
fails: Nesting hides frequently-used destinations behind an extra click; keep hot paths at the top level.

claim: Always give the current route a visible active state — a filled or tinted rounded rectangle behind the whole link row is a reliable default.
why: Without it users lose track of where they are in the product; a full-row background is more legible than a thin bar or a colour-only label change.
when: Every navigational sidebar.

claim: Treat leftover vertical space in the sidebar as a slot for one deliberate extra block — a feature promo, a search entry point, or a notification feed — not as padding to fill.
why: The space is already persistent and in view, so it's efficient placement for something ambient; framing it as optional keeps it from crowding navigation.
when: Tall sidebars with a short link list and real empty space below it.
fails: Adding blocks when the nav already fills the column, or stacking several promos — the extra content then competes with the sidebar's primary job.

claim: Put an action in a popover when it has few controls and no destructive commit — settings toggles, display options, quick filters — and let clicking outside dismiss it with the change already applied.
why: Lightweight, reversible choices don't warrant taking over the screen or forcing an explicit confirmation; a non-blocking surface keeps the user's flow intact.
when: The control set is small and each change is independently reversible or auto-saved.
fails: The interaction has multiple dependent fields, validation, or an irreversible commit — dismissing by clicking away would then destroy or half-apply work.

claim: Use a modal when the task is complex but its subject is what's already on screen — for example, creating a new item in the list the user is looking at — so the user never loses their place in the data.
why: Keeping the creation flow anchored to the page preserves the mental link between the form and the collection it feeds.
when: The new context is a child of, or directly operates on, the currently displayed content.
fails: The task is unrelated to the current view, or is large enough that the surrounding page is irrelevant — route to a page instead.

claim: Treat a modal as blocking: require an explicit primary action or cancel to close it, and do not let an outside click silently discard entered data.
why: A modal implies a committed decision; ambiguous dismissal risks losing multi-field input the user has invested effort in.
when: Any modal containing a form or a state-changing operation.
fails: Trivial single-choice or read-only modals, where forcing a button press is friction without benefit.

claim: Fire a toast confirming the result immediately after a modal closes.
why: The modal covered the page while the change was made, so the user has no way to see that the underlying content updated; the toast supplies the missing feedback.
when: Any overlay that obscures the region it mutates.
fails: When the change is fully visible on close — a new row visibly appearing in the list can be its own confirmation, making the toast redundant noise.

claim: Route warnings and errors through the toast system rather than inventing per-screen error surfaces, and use toasts for anything the user should notice without surrendering the whole screen.
why: Warning and error states are the states teams most often forget to design; a single ambient channel guarantees they have somewhere to appear.
when: Non-blocking system feedback: success confirmations, background failures, warnings, and light prompts to act.
fails: Errors the user must resolve before continuing, or messages that need to persist — a transient toast will be missed.

claim: Promote an interaction to its own route when the context is large or long-lived — opening an existing record for detailed work rather than creating a small new one.
why: Big or persistent contexts need room, a shareable URL, and browser history semantics that an overlay cannot provide.
when: Detail views, editors, or anything the user may stay in for an extended period.
fails: Short, focused tasks — routing away for a two-field form is unnecessary navigation cost.

claim: Every drilled-into page must ship with an explicit return path — a back button or a breadcrumb trail — placed before the page content.
why: Overlays have an obvious dismiss affordance; a route does not, so the way back must be built in rather than left to the browser button.
when: Any page reached by drilling down from a list or dashboard view.

claim: Choose the container by escalating along two axes — context complexity and context permanence — from popover to modal to full page, and treat each step up as also stepping up how much the user is interrupted.
why: The three surfaces form a deliberate ladder; matching weight of container to weight of task avoids both over- and under-interrupting.
when: Deciding where any new dashboard action should live.

claim: Design the display layer and the action layer as separate passes: build the read views first, then audit each one for the actions it implies and assign a container to every one.
why: A dashboard that only renders information is incomplete — the ability to act on what's shown is the actual product.
when: Building a dashboard from scratch.

claim: When navigation labels are product codes, model numbers, or invented names that carry no meaning to a first-time visitor, attach an identifying image to each nav item so the image, not the label, does the work of communicating what the item is.
why: A visitor who cannot decode a name cannot choose; an image conveys product category (truck vs. SUV, etc.) instantly and without prior brand knowledge, removing a comprehension step from the entry point of the site.
when: Navigation or menu items whose labels are opaque to newcomers — SKU-style model names, internal jargon, brand-invented product lines, or catalogues where items differ visually in ways names don't capture.
fails: Not addressed directly; the chapter only endorses adding images. Implied limit: when labels are already self-explanatory, images add weight without adding meaning.

claim: Choose nav imagery that shows the actual thing at a recognisable angle and scale, so the category is legible at thumbnail size — a side or three-quarter product shot rather than a cropped detail or abstract graphic.
why: The image only replaces the label if a glance resolves it; the payoff described is being able to tell one product type from another without reading, which requires the whole object to be visible in a small frame.
when: Any nav thumbnail whose job is identification rather than decoration.

claim: Decorative imagery in a dropdown is still worth adding even when it identifies nothing specific, because it breaks up a wall of text links and gives the menu visual interest.
why: A menu that expands into nothing but a text list feels flat and unrewarding; imagery gives the panel presence and makes opening it feel like arriving somewhere.
when: Large mega-menus or full-width dropdown panels with room to spare beside the link list.
fails: Not addressed; the presenter concedes these images aren't specific to anything, which implies they earn their place on atmosphere alone and would not survive in a compact or utility nav.

claim: Treat the navigation as a first-time-visitor comprehension surface, not just a routing surface — design it for someone who arrived cold and has no vocabulary for your products yet.
why: The whole argument is framed from the position of a person landing on the page who doesn't know what any of the names mean; nav that assumes existing product knowledge fails exactly the audience you're trying to convert.
when: Marketing, ecommerce, and product-catalogue sites where a meaningful share of traffic is new.
fails: Internal tools, dashboards, or apps for returning users, where familiar labels are faster than images and the extra weight slows navigation.

claim: Where imagery is the primary identifier, let visitors choose by appearance rather than forcing a read-and-decide step — mirror the picture-menu pattern where a good-looking photo is enough to commit.
why: The restaurant analogy makes the point that picking from photos is low-effort and reliably satisfying; the same holds for products where visual appeal drives the decision.
when: Categories where the item's look is a genuine part of the decision — vehicles, food, furniture, apparel, travel destinations.
fails: Decisions driven by specs, price, or compatibility, where a photo can flatter an item that's wrong for the visitor's needs.

claim: Give every screen exactly one job, and cut any module that does not serve that job — a settings screen shows settings only, an editor edits only.
why: Mobile viewports are too small to host competing tasks; extra modules push the primary task down the screen and dilute what the user came to do.
when: Designing or auditing any interior screen of a mobile app.
fails: Hub screens like home, dashboards, or feeds, whose actual job is aggregation across many features.

claim: When new functionality needs to be added, route it to a new destination rather than densifying the layout of an existing screen.
why: Adding a page preserves the single-purpose contract of each screen, whereas adding a section to an existing screen erodes it and compounds over time.
when: Scope grows on a screen that already has a clear primary task.
fails: The new function is a short sub-task of the current task, where full navigation would break the user's context — use an overlay instead.

claim: Do not stack secondary modules such as recent items, suggestions, or promoted templates above the primary content of a focused screen.
why: They compete for the top of the viewport, which is the most valuable space and should belong to the screen's one job.
when: Editors, detail screens, and settings screens.
fails: Home and browse screens where recommendation modules are the point.

claim: Use a bottom sheet when a sub-task must be completed without abandoning the current screen — picking a template while writing, choosing an option while editing.
why: A sheet layers over the current screen so the underlying task stays visible and mentally alive; a full page navigation severs that continuity.
when: A sub-task that is short, returns a value to the current screen, and would not survive a context switch.
fails: The sub-task is long, multi-step, or a destination in its own right — that deserves a real page.

claim: Size a bottom sheet to its content rather than a fixed height, from a small options list to near-full-screen.
why: Height is a free variable in this pattern, so it should be spent on making the content readable rather than matching an arbitrary standard.
when: Any bottom sheet, from a two-item action list to a searchable picker.

claim: Structure a content-heavy bottom sheet with a title, a search field, explicit confirm and dismiss controls, and then the scrollable content.
why: Once a sheet holds enough items to require scanning, the user needs orientation, filtering, and an unambiguous way to commit or back out.
when: Sheets containing a list or grid the user must choose from.
fails: Small action sheets, where a title and confirm/cancel chrome is more furniture than the content warrants.

claim: Make bottom sheets dismissible and adjustable by drag gesture, not only by tapping a close control.
why: Sheets sit at the bottom of the screen inside thumb reach, so gesture handling is the fastest way in and out.
when: Any overlay anchored to the bottom edge on touch devices.

claim: Let a primary add button either reveal a small menu of creation options or drop the user straight into an input, instead of navigating to a separate creation screen.
why: Creation is a frequent, low-ceremony action; resolving it in place keeps the user on the screen that gave them the intent.
when: List, feed, and collection screens with a floating or docked add affordance.
fails: Creation requires substantial structured input, which warrants a dedicated screen.

claim: Before choosing a pattern, decide whether the user can afford to leave the current screen; that answer picks between navigation and an overlay.
why: Context cost, not visual preference, is the deciding variable — the same feature belongs on a page in one flow and in a sheet in another.
when: Any time a screen needs to expose a secondary action.

claim: When designing an unfamiliar flow or component, study how several shipping apps have solved it before drawing your own version.
why: Established patterns carry accumulated usability decisions that are cheaper to adopt than to rediscover.
when: Onboarding flows, common components, and any pattern with widespread precedent.
fails: Copying precedent uncritically when your product's constraints genuinely differ.

claim: Design the zero-content version of every screen that can hold user-generated content, not just the populated 'ideal' version.
why: A populated mockup is the last state a real user reaches, not the first; shipping only that leaves the actual first-run experience undesigned.
when: Any list, feed, inbox, calendar, or collection whose contents come from the user.
fails: Screens with system-supplied or always-present content, where a zero state is unreachable.

claim: For a first-run empty state, use one full-screen state that points at the single primary action rather than several per-category prompt cards.
why: Multiple invitations split attention and reintroduce a decision at the moment the user has the least context; one target makes the next step unambiguous.
when: First login or an emptied collection where the app has one dominant create action.
fails: The app has several genuinely distinct entry paths with no dominant one, or onboarding requires a real choice (e.g. import vs. start fresh) before anything can be created.

claim: Anchor the first-run empty state to the primary action control already in the interface (e.g. the FAB or plus button) instead of introducing a separate one-off button.
why: It teaches the control the user will keep using afterwards, so the lesson survives past the empty state.
when: The interface has a persistent primary-action affordance.
fails: The primary action lives behind a nested or contextual menu the user cannot see from the empty screen.

claim: Pair the first-run empty state with a short popover or coach mark that explains the interaction model in a sentence, and show it only on first run.
why: Empty artwork alone conveys 'nothing here' but not 'here is how this works'; a small instruction closes that gap without a full tutorial flow.
when: First session, when the mental model of the app is not yet formed.
fails: Repeated on every visit, or stacked into a multi-step tour — it becomes a dismissal chore.

claim: Treat 'no search results' as a distinct empty state from 'no content yet', with different copy and different actions.
why: The two states have opposite causes — one means the user has not created anything, the other means their query missed existing content — so an invitation to create is the wrong response to a failed search.
when: Any search, filter, or query surface over user content.

claim: Build a no-results state from four parts: an illustration, an explicit acknowledgement that nothing matched the entered keywords, one or more suggested alternative queries, and a clear way out of the state.
why: The illustration softens a dead end, the acknowledgement confirms the search actually ran, suggestions cover typos and near-misses, and the exit action stops the user from being stranded on a blank screen.
when: Search returns zero matches.
fails: Very sparse result sets where an illustration crowds out the few results that do exist, or when no plausible suggestion can be generated and a fake one would mislead.

claim: Echo the user's actual query back in the no-results message rather than showing a generic 'nothing found'.
why: Naming the keywords lets the user spot their own typo immediately and confirms the system searched what they meant.
when: Text-entry search where the query is short enough to display inline.
fails: Long or pasted queries that would overflow the message; truncate instead.

claim: Give every empty state an exit — a button that clears the search, resets filters, or returns to the full list.
why: Without an escape the user has to re-derive how they got there, which is the main way a no-results screen becomes a dead end.
when: Any state reached by narrowing content down.

claim: Before choosing any component, write the user's intent as a single verb phrase ("find a place to stay on these dates"), then let that sentence dictate which controls exist on the screen.
why: Components chosen from the intent are guaranteed to be load-bearing; components chosen from visual instinct have to justify themselves after the fact and usually can't.
when: Starting any new flow, screen, or feature where the layout is not yet fixed.
fails: Intent is genuinely unknown or contested — then research or a bet on a hypothesis has to come first, and the sentence is a placeholder rather than a brief.

claim: Make the primary intent's control the first element you place and the largest thing on the screen; everything else is added around it.
why: The element that does the job the user came for should be the one they cannot miss; ordering the design work this way makes visual hierarchy fall out of function instead of being imposed on top of it.
when: Landing pages and entry screens with one dominant task, such as search-led marketplaces.
fails: Screens with several equally weighted tasks, or dashboards where no single action dominates.

claim: Expand a primary control only with the parameters the intent itself requires — for accommodation search that is destination, dates, and traveller count — and reject any field that does not narrow the result set.
why: Each parameter is a question the user must answer; only questions that change what comes back are worth asking.
when: Designing search, booking, or query-shaped inputs.
fails: Domains where a legally or operationally required field must be collected even though it does not affect results.

claim: Test every proposed addition with the question "what can the user now do that they could not do before?" — if the answer is nothing, the addition is decoration and should be cut or explicitly justified on non-functional grounds.
why: Additions accumulate by default because each one looks plausible in isolation; a single functional test applied consistently is what stops drift.
when: Reviewing any iteration where the screen has grown — hero images, headers, badges, illustrations, extra cards.
fails: The addition's job is genuinely non-functional and stated as such: brand tone, trust signalling, or orienting a first-time visitor. The test then becomes whether it earns its space against that goal, not whether it adds capability.

claim: Do not treat a hero header with a background image as a default requirement for a landing screen; place it only after the functional layout works without it.
why: The pattern is copied so widely that it gets added reflexively, and it competes for the space the primary control needs.
when: Marketplace, tool, and utility landing pages where the user arrives with a task.
fails: Marketing or brand-first pages where persuasion, not task completion, is the actual intent being served.

claim: Enumerate more than one user intent per screen and design a distinct affordance for each: searchers get a query input, browsers get a visible listing grid.
why: Users arrive at the same URL in different states of decidedness; serving only the most decided one strands everyone else.
when: Any entry point serving a mixed audience — first-time and returning, decided and undecided.
fails: Focused sub-flows deep in a funnel, where intent has already been narrowed and extra paths are noise.

claim: When you serve a browse intent, pair the listing with filtering controls rather than shipping an unfiltered feed.
why: "I don't know where" is rarely total indecision — the user still has constraints like budget, dates, or property type, and filters let them converge without having to formulate a query.
when: Any browse or discovery surface with more results than a user will scan.
fails: Small or curated result sets where filters add chrome without reducing effort.

claim: Treat fonts, colours, and icons as changes to perception, not to capability — never let a visual revision stand in for a functional one, and never count it as progress on a functional problem.
why: Restyling produces a strong feeling of improvement while the interface does exactly what it did before, which is how teams polish their way past an unsolved usability problem.
when: Iteration reviews and critique, especially when a design 'feels better' but user outcomes have not moved.
fails: Problems that genuinely are perceptual — legibility, contrast, scannability, affordance clarity — where a visual change is the correct fix.

claim: Gate feature growth on intent growth: add a new UI element only when you can name the new or unserved user intent it exists to satisfy.
why: It gives feature requests a falsifiable admission test and keeps the interface's complexity proportional to the range of jobs it actually does.
when: Scoping features and reviewing additions across the life of a product.
fails: Infrastructure-driven or compliance-driven requirements that no user asked for but the product must carry.

claim: Rank every control in a view by access frequency and importance, then assign it a visibility level: always-visible for primary, revealed-on-interaction (hover, swipe, popover, menu) for secondary, buried in settings for rare.
why: Screen real estate and user attention are finite; giving a rarely used control permanent presence spends both on something most users will not touch, and dilutes the controls that matter.
when: Designing any dense surface — dashboards, data tables, list rows, toolbars — where more actions exist than can be shown at equal weight.
fails: Frequency is misjudged, or the action is destructive/legally required/accessibility-critical, in which case hiding it behind an interaction makes it undiscoverable to the people who need it most.

claim: Treat explicitness as a continuous scale rather than a show/hide binary: hover-only icon < always-visible icon < icon with visible text label < dedicated always-visible button. Move a control up or down this scale to tune its prominence instead of deleting it.
why: Naming intermediate steps gives you calibrated adjustments — you can make something more findable without promoting it to a top-level control, or reduce clutter without removing the affordance entirely.
when: You have decided a control belongs in a view but are choosing how loudly to present it.
fails: The interaction that reveals the control does not exist on the target device — hover has no equivalent on touch, so a hover-only control effectively drops off the scale rather than sitting low on it.

claim: Handle a secondary flow in an overlay anchored to its trigger (popover, sheet, inline panel) rather than navigating the user to a separate page.
why: Navigating away destroys the user's place and context for a task that is a brief detour from their real work; an overlay keeps the originating view intact behind it.
when: A short, self-contained task — sharing, filtering, quick edits — branches off a main view the user intends to return to.
fails: The flow is long, multi-step, or needs substantial space; then a full page or dedicated route is the honest container.

claim: Within a revealed container like a popover, apply the same visibility ranking again: put the container's single primary action at the top, always visible and focused, and demote everything else.
why: Opening a surface does not flatten hierarchy — a popover with three equally weighted controls forces the user to re-read a UI they opened to do one specific thing.
when: Any nested surface — modal, popover, drawer, menu — containing more than one action.

claim: When a hover- or gesture-revealed control is an icon with no label, pair it with a tooltip that names the action.
why: Reducing explicitness by removing the label removes meaning; the tooltip restores it at the moment the user has already signalled interest, without the permanent space cost of visible text.
when: Space-constrained rows or cells where icon-only secondary actions appear on interaction.
fails: Touch contexts where there is no hover state to trigger a tooltip, and for destructive actions where a bare icon plus tooltip is too thin a signal before an irreversible change.

claim: Reveal secondary row actions on the interaction the user performs when they go looking for them (hover on pointer, swipe on touch), and keep the row's single most common action directly tappable without any reveal.
why: The most frequent action should cost zero interactions; everything else can cost one, because reaching for it is itself evidence of intent.
when: Repeating list or table rows with one dominant action and several supporting ones.
fails: The reveal gesture is undiscoverable with no visual affordance hinting it exists, leaving users unaware the actions are there at all.

claim: Build onboarding as a sequence of one-step-at-a-time prompts tied to the real UI — a single tooltip on the most important action, then the next step, or a persistent corner checklist — rather than a welcome modal that explains the whole product at once.
why: A multi-bullet modal is read (if at all) with no context to attach the information to and is forgotten on dismiss; in-place sequenced prompts arrive at the moment the user can act on them and leave a persistent trace they can return to.
when: A first-time user lands on a feature-dense product surface and needs a starting point.
fails: The sequence is applied to trivial or self-evident UI, where step-by-step coaching becomes an obstacle between the user and the product.

claim: Distinguish sequencing from hiding: progressive disclosure defers when a capability is surfaced, it does not remove the capability or make it reachable only through the onboarding flow.
why: Users who skip or dismiss the guided path must still be able to find everything; if the only route to a feature is a one-time prompt, dismissing it becomes a permanent loss of function.
when: Designing onboarding, empty states, or any staged reveal of features.

claim: Calibrate these judgements by studying large volumes of shipped software rather than reasoning from first principles alone — collect real screens of the pattern you are designing before designing it.
why: Where a control belongs on the explicitness spectrum is a convention-sensitive call; seeing how many real products resolved the same tension is faster and more reliable than deriving it.
when: Designing a pattern — onboarding, sharing, row actions — that is well established across existing products.
fails: Copying the consensus pattern where your product's frequency and importance ranking genuinely differs from theirs.

claim: In a settings or configuration panel, show only the options most users need on first view and put the rest behind a collapsed 'advanced' disclosure that is closed by default.
why: An always-expanded wall of controls reads as unconsidered and dated; collapsing the long tail cuts visual noise without removing capability.
when: Panels, cards, and forms where the option set is uneven — a few common controls plus many rarely-touched ones.
fails: When the 'advanced' bucket is used as a dumping ground for controls people actually reach for every session, or when it hides a setting required to complete the primary task, which turns one glance into a hunt.

claim: Before restyling a UI, list the actions a user would reasonably want in that surface and add any that have no control at all — e.g. switching between two output formats, or attaching a description.
why: Visual polish on an incomplete feature set still leaves the product feeling thin; missing affordances are a design defect, not a backlog item.
when: Reviewing a generated or first-draft interface for a feature that has more than one meaningful mode or optional metadata.
fails: When it becomes an excuse to bolt on every conceivable option, re-creating the clutter that progressive disclosure was meant to solve.

claim: Choose a layout structure that has an obvious empty slot pattern — a repeatable row, field group, or card cell — so a new option can be added later without redesigning the container.
why: Extensibility is a property of the layout itself; a rigid one-off arrangement forces a full rework the first time the feature set grows.
when: Designing panels for features you expect to expand — settings, integrations, per-item configuration.
fails: When the generic slot grid is so neutral that it flattens hierarchy and every option reads as equally important.

claim: When improving an AI-generated interface, spend your first and largest effort on layout and card composition rather than on colour, copy, or micro-styling.
why: Generation models produce competent atoms but weak arrangement, so structural fixes carry the biggest visible delta per unit of effort.
when: Triaging a vibe-coded or scaffolded UI with limited time to improve it.
fails: When the underlying structure is already sound and the actual problems are spacing, type scale, or contrast — restructuring then costs time for no gain.

claim: Judge a redesign by whether the arrangement changed, not by whether the surface changed — moving controls into groups and tiers is the edit that reads as 'designed'.
why: The chapter's before/after is framed entirely in terms of grouping, disclosure, and slot structure; no colour or type change is cited as the source of improvement.
when: Critiquing your own or a generated UI and deciding what to change first.

claim: Before designing, audit five to ten direct competitors and explicitly note which patterns are shared by all of them; treat any pattern that appears everywhere as a cliché to deliberately decide about, not a default to inherit.
why: A whole category converging on one layout usually means people copied the leader rather than solved the problem, so inheriting it produces a site indistinguishable from its rivals.
when: Starting a redesign or a new site in a category with an obvious market leader.
fails: The shared pattern is a genuine usability convention (cart icon top-right, logo links home) — familiarity there is a feature, and breaking it costs the user.

claim: Do not build a page whose only job is to funnel users to another page; if a page has one section and one outbound link, merge its content into the destination.
why: A page that carries no information of its own adds a click and a load without adding value; structure should move users toward content, not through empty rooms.
when: Any page in the site map that contains a single hero or section and exists mainly as a gateway.
fails: The page is a genuine routing hub for several distinct destinations (a category index, a role selector), where the choice itself is the content.

claim: When the company sells essentially one product, delete the marketing homepage and make the product page the site root.
why: A homepage earns its place by helping users choose between offerings; with nothing to choose between, it only delays the pitch the visitor came for.
when: Single-product or single-model companies, especially where the current homepage just teases the product.
fails: The brand has multiple product lines, distinct audience segments, or needs a homepage to carry news, investor and recruiting signals.

claim: Secondary pages that lose their homepage entry point should stay reachable from the nav bar rather than being surfaced as sections on the main page.
why: Removing a hub page must not remove discoverability; the nav absorbs the wayfinding job the homepage used to do while keeping the main page focused.
when: Consolidating a site map by collapsing pages together.

claim: Use imagery inside the nav dropdown — thumbnail each destination instead of listing text links alone.
why: For visual products, a picture identifies the destination faster than its name and lets the nav do some of the selling.
when: Product-led sites where the items in the nav are visually distinguishable things (vehicles, plans, hardware, collections).
fails: Destinations are abstract or near-identical visually, where photos add weight without aiding recognition.

claim: Keep the existing page's content order as the base for the redesign and change it only where you have a stated reason.
why: The current sequence encodes decisions that may already work; wholesale reordering adds risk and hides which change caused which result.
when: Redesigning a live site rather than designing from scratch.
fails: The existing order is itself the diagnosed problem.

claim: When merging pages, add substantive sections (mission, editorial or blog) so the resulting single page still has narrative depth rather than just a hero and a spec sheet.
why: Collapsing pages removes surface area; without new material the remaining page reads as thin, which is the same failure as the single-section site being criticised.
when: After consolidating a site map down to one or two primary pages.
fails: Sections are added purely as filler with no real content behind them, which lengthens the scroll without rewarding it.

claim: Judge a site on whether its structure makes sense before judging its visuals; a well-executed page can still be the wrong page.
why: Craft cannot rescue an information architecture that wastes the user's clicks, so structure is the first review pass.
when: Critiquing or auditing any existing site.

claim: In a navigation dropdown, pair each destination with a supporting visual — a thumbnail, product icon, or screenshot — rather than shipping a bare column of text links.
why: An image gives the eye something to land on and makes the menu feel considered; a wall of undifferentiated link text is visually flat and offers no signal about what sits behind each label.
when: Multi-item navigation menus where labels alone are ambiguous — product suites, feature lists, resource hubs, solution pages.
fails: Navigation with two or three self-evident items, where imagery adds weight and load time without resolving any ambiguity.

claim: Give every nav item enough supporting context — a short descriptor line or preview image — that the user can predict the destination page before clicking.
why: A link label on its own is a guess; adding context converts navigation from trial-and-error clicking into an informed choice, which reduces bounce-backs to the menu.
when: Any site where nav labels are branded, abstract, or internally-coined names rather than plain descriptions.
fails: Utility navigation using universally understood labels (Pricing, Login, Contact), where added description is noise.

claim: Scale the dropdown to the size of the site: use a full-width multi-column panel when there is a genuinely large product surface, and a single compact card-style panel when there isn't.
why: The pattern's value is contextual preview, not size; a sprawling mega-menu over a thin catalogue reads as padding, while a small enriched panel still delivers the professional feel.
when: Choosing dropdown architecture during nav design for sites of any catalogue size.
fails: Copying an enterprise mega-menu structure onto a small site purely because a large competitor uses one.

claim: Design the dropdown as a laid-out surface with its own grouping, hierarchy, and spacing — treat it as a small page region rather than an unstyled list container.
why: Once images and descriptions enter the menu, list-default styling can't carry the density; the panel needs sections, alignment, and breathing room to stay scannable.
when: Building enriched navigation menus that contain more than a handful of mixed-media items.

claim: Prefer navigation patterns that solve a comprehension problem over ones that are merely current, and expect those to survive past the season.
why: A pattern that reduces user uncertainty has a functional reason to persist, while a purely stylistic trend has nothing anchoring it once fashion moves.
when: Deciding which contemporary design trends to adopt into a long-lived product.
fails: Using longevity as a rationalisation to adopt a heavy pattern the site's scale doesn't justify.

claim: Before restyling any screen, audit hierarchy and delete elements; treat removal as the first and cheapest layout fix, not a last resort.
why: Most crowding is caused by elements that never earned their place; cutting them frees space without requiring any new design decisions.
when: Redesigning an existing dense interface, especially a dashboard where content competes for one viewport.
fails: Elements look redundant but serve distinct user roles or permission states you can't see in a static mock — verify function before cutting.

claim: Check where the fold lands and, if primary content falls below it, reclaim vertical space from chrome rather than accepting the scroll.
why: Scrolling is acceptable, but not when the space above the fold is spent on navigation and identity rather than the data the user came for.
when: Dashboards and data-first screens where the top-priority content should be visible on load.
fails: Long-form or feed content where scrolling is the expected primary interaction and a tall header is a deliberate entry moment.

claim: Move persistent global controls — logo, menu, account, settings, add-content — from a horizontal top bar into a vertical sidebar.
why: A sidebar consumes horizontal space, which dashboards usually have more of, and returns vertical space to the content; it also gives navigation a natural home.
when: Wide-viewport applications with a fixed set of global destinations and vertically hungry content.
fails: Narrow or mobile viewports, or content that itself needs full width (wide tables, timelines), where a collapsed or bottom nav serves better.

claim: Delete any label that only restates what the screen visibly is; do not title an interface with its own category name.
why: If the content makes the product's purpose obvious, the label carries zero information and only consumes prime space.
when: Page titles or headers on single-purpose screens where the content is self-evident.
fails: Multi-context apps where the same shell hosts different sections and the title is the user's only orientation cue.

claim: When two controls appear to do the same job, keep one and remove the other rather than differentiating them.
why: Duplicate affordances force the user to decide which one is correct, which is a cost with no matching benefit.
when: Auditing a header or toolbar that has accumulated controls over time.
fails: The two controls genuinely differ in scope (global search vs. filter-within-table) — then the fix is labelling and placement, not deletion.

claim: Cut affordances that don't match how the domain is actually used, even when they're technically functional.
why: Domain-implausible features (voice dictation in a finance tool) add visual noise and imply capabilities nobody exercises.
when: Evaluating inherited feature sets against the realistic behaviour of the product's users.
fails: Accessibility affordances, which can look domain-odd but serve users who depend on them — never cut these on plausibility grounds.

claim: If content is important enough to be a header action, promote it to a persistent on-screen section instead of hiding it behind a button.
why: A click-to-reveal panel signals the content is secondary; if the user needs it every session, the interaction is a tax.
when: High-frequency, glanceable content like tasks, alerts, or an activity feed on a dashboard.
fails: The content is long, occasional, or contextual — persisting it starves the primary content of space.

claim: Make single-entity UI reflect its real multiplicity: if a screen shows one team member, show several plus a control to manage the set.
why: A lone avatar implies an incomplete data model; showing a group communicates the actual scope of the feature and reveals the management action it needs.
when: Any UI element representing a collection that the mock has populated with a single item.
fails: The entity really is singular (the account owner, the current user) — pluralising it invents a feature.

claim: Order sidebar items by frequency and permanence: brand at the top, primary navigation next, people/context below, and low-frequency settings anchored to the bottom.
why: The top and bottom edges are the two most findable positions; reserving the bottom for settings keeps it reachable without competing with daily navigation.
when: Building a vertical navigation rail with a mix of high- and low-frequency destinations.

claim: Design the collapsed state of a sidebar at the same time as the expanded one, not afterwards.
why: The collapsed rail is what forces the icon set and the item ordering to be self-sufficient without labels; discovering this late means reworking the structure.
when: Any navigation intended to collapse or adapt across widths.

claim: Give demoted-but-not-deleted elements a conditional slot: mark them 'add back if space remains' rather than fighting for them up front.
why: Deferring low-value elements keeps the audit moving and lets the final layout, not early attachment, decide whether they fit.
when: Elements like timestamps or dates that are mildly useful but not load-bearing.

claim: Place form field labels above their inputs as persistent text; never use the placeholder attribute as the label.
why: Placeholder labels vanish the moment the user starts typing, so anyone who pauses, gets interrupted, or reviews before submitting has no way to tell what each field wants.
when: Any form with more than one input, especially modals and signup flows where fields look similar (email, password, confirm password).
fails: Not addressed in the chapter; in practice a single obvious search field can survive on placeholder text alone.

claim: Use the placeholder slot for a concrete example of the expected value (e.g. a sample email address or name format), not for repeating the field name.
why: An example previews the format before the user commits to typing, reducing entry errors and hesitation.
when: Fields where the expected format is ambiguous or worth demonstrating.
fails: Not addressed; example text set too dark can be mistaken for a filled value.

claim: Give the modal an explicit heading naming the action it performs ('Create account'), so its purpose is readable without inspecting the fields.
why: Signup and login modals share almost identical form layouts; without a title the user has to infer which one they're in.
when: Any modal whose layout is near-identical to a sibling flow — signup vs login, edit vs duplicate.

claim: Include a visible route to the opposite flow inside the modal — a small 'Log in' link on a signup modal, and vice versa.
why: A large share of users hitting the signup modal already have an account; without an exit they must dismiss the modal and hunt for the other entry point.
when: Paired authentication flows or any modal that a user might have opened by mistake.

claim: When you add label text above inputs, increase the vertical gaps between field groups rather than keeping the original spacing.
why: Each field now occupies two stacked text elements, so the previous rhythm reads as cramped and the label/input pairing stops being visually obvious.
when: Any time content is added inside an existing stack layout.

claim: Snap every spacing, padding, and size value in a modal to a 4px grid.
why: A fixed increment keeps gaps consistent across the form and makes spacing decisions mechanical instead of eyeballed.
when: Signup, login, and similar compact modal layouts; extends to UI layout generally.
fails: Not addressed; typography line-height and optical alignment sometimes need off-grid values.

claim: Style input fields with a subtle off-white fill and a border at roughly 40% opacity instead of a white fill with a full-strength stroke.
why: The fill marks the field as an interactive target without a hard outline, and the lightened border stops the form from reading as a grid of heavy boxes competing with the content.
when: Text inputs in light-theme forms and modals.
fails: Contrast-sensitive contexts — a low-opacity border can drop below accessible contrast for field boundaries; and off-white fill fails if the modal background is already off-white.

claim: Design the signup modal as a template that scales — adding or removing fields and swapping the heading and CTA should convert it into a login modal without a new layout.
why: Auth modals share structure, so one well-spaced, grid-aligned pattern covers the whole family.
when: Building an auth or form component set.

claim: Judge a form on whether it survives being used, not on how it looks in a static, empty state.
why: The starting example looked presentable but broke as soon as a user typed — the failure only appears in the filled state.
when: Reviewing any input-heavy interface.

claim: Group a long, story-like recap into a small set of clearly named thematic chapters so people can navigate by intent.
why: Chapter labels let people jump directly to the type of insight they want instead of progressing through the entire sequence.
when: A personalized recap or multi-part experience contains distinct content categories.
fails: The content is too short or the categories overlap enough that separate destinations add unnecessary navigation.

claim: Provide a persistent, low-profile chapter picker near the bottom of the screen to support quick non-linear navigation.
why: It gives users an easy way to skip to a desired section without abandoning the immersive full-screen format.
when: Users are viewing sequential full-screen content but may want to revisit or bypass sections.
fails: Bottom controls conflict with essential gestures, platform navigation, or other primary actions.

claim: Create a dedicated summary dashboard that consolidates the most important statistics and makes them easy to share.
why: A summary offers a practical overview without forcing users to leave the recap experience.
when: The experience produces multiple metrics that benefit from review or social sharing.
fails: The summary merely duplicates every screen without prioritizing useful headline information.

claim: Use one primary share entry point when several sharing scopes are available, then let users choose the scope in a follow-up menu.
why: Separate nearby controls for similar sharing actions create uncertainty about which control to use.
when: A flow can share a single item, a grouped section, or an entire multi-step experience.

claim: Offer sharing at the natural content levels of the experience: individual screen, section, and complete recap.
why: People may want to highlight one result, send a meaningful subset, or share the whole narrative.
when: Content is organized into independently meaningful screens and chapters.

claim: Label shared aggregate views with the original user's identity.
why: A recipient opening someone else's personalized content needs immediate ownership context.
when: Shared content contains personal data, preferences, results, or recommendations that could be mistaken for the recipient's own.

claim: In financial-product onboarding, pair a bank-connection request with clear reassurance about security and misuse of funds.
why: Connecting financial accounts creates immediate trust friction that can prevent activation.
when: The product requests access to banking, payments, or other sensitive financial data early in the flow.
fails: Reassurance is vague or substitutes for concrete security, privacy, and consent information.

claim: Show users personalized or representative value before asking them to complete a goal-setting action.
why: Spending insights establish why the product is useful before it asks for more effort or commitment.
when: An app can derive meaningful data-based insights during onboarding.
fails: The insight preview is empty, misleading, or delays a required setup step without adding value.

claim: Use a swipeable sequence of concise insight cards to introduce multiple data points without crowding one onboarding screen.
why: Separate cards let users absorb a spending breakdown and monthly average progressively.
when: Several related metrics need to be explained during onboarding.
fails: The metrics must be compared directly at once or the interaction is not discoverable.

claim: Make savings-goal setup capture both the user’s existing savings and their target timeframe.
why: Starting progress and deadline define the baseline and pace needed for a goal-oriented experience.
when: The product helps users plan toward a measurable financial target.
fails: The goal is not time-bound or users need more flexible planning inputs than a fixed period.

claim: Use an adjustable control such as a slider for selecting a bounded goal duration.
why: It provides a quick, visual way to tune a numeric timeframe during a simple setup flow.
when: The allowable period has a sensible limited range and approximate adjustment is acceptable.
fails: Users need precise values, broad ranges, or accessible text entry as the primary interaction.

claim: Reassess the visual theme after reviewing the complete onboarding flow, and change it when the first direction does not support the intended product feel.
why: A full-flow review can reveal that a different contrast and mood, such as dark mode, better serves the design.
when: The visual system is still early enough to revise before detailed product implementation.
fails: A theme switch is made without checking accessibility, user preference, and downstream component impact.
